cognate: Gk ἄμβροτος = Ved. amṛ́ta- < *n̥-mr̥-tó-; Gk ἕννυμι/ἕσσαν, εἷμα = Ved. vas- 'clothe' < *wes-
drift_or_renewal: Vedic uses the substantivized neuter amṛ́tam ('the immortal', ambrosia) as the garment itself (instr./acc.), Greek puts ἄμβροτος on the garment noun (εἵματα, itself *wes-men-); Greek also has the substantive ἀμβροσίη alongside in Il. 16.670/680
review: Passages read as claimed: HyAphr 6 and Il. 16.670/680, Od. 24.59, 7.265 have the stock Greek line with ἄμβροτα + εἵματα + a form of ἕννυμι; RV 6.75.18b (= AVŚ 7.118.1) has amŕ̥tena with the imperative vastām of vas- 'wear, clothe' (the automatic mapping to h₂wes- 'dwell' is wrong; the claim's reading is right); AVŚ 9.1.2 has amṛtam with the participle vasānāṃ. Etymology exact: amŕ̥ta- = ἄμβροτος (*n̥-mr̥-tó-), vas- = ἕννυμι/εἷμα (*wes-). The relation is congruent at the level 'clothe (a body) in/with the immortal': Greek puts the adjective on the garment noun, Vedic uses the substantivised neuter as the covering, and Greek has the substantive ἀμβροσίῃ beside it in Il. 16.670/680, so the drift is defensible. Context is close: a body made inviolable or divine by what it is dressed or anointed with (Sarpedon's corpse; the warrior's armour charm). Not derivative. Caveats: the Vedic side is a single collocation (RV has amŕ̥ta- + vas- 2 together only here and 2.10.1c), and ἄμβροτος is a very common epithet, hence medium generic risk.

Iuppiter (not in slab word list; supplied by reader)

cognate: Gk Ζεύς = Ved. dyáuḥ (dyú-/div-) = Lat. Iu- (Iou-) < *dyḗws; Gk πατήρ = Ved. pitā́ = Lat. -piter/pater < *ph₂tḗr
drift_or_renewal: none in the lexemes; Latin has univerbated the phrase into one name (Iuppiter < voc. *dyeu-pater), with the inflected oblique built on Iou- (Ioui in the same Cato passages); Greek and Vedic keep two words, freely separable (Ζεὺς ὀμώμοται πατήρ; dyaur naḥ pitā)
phrase: *dyēus ph₂tēr 'Father Sky': Ζεὺς ... πατήρ ~ dyaur ... pitā ~ Iupiter
review: Passages checked: Eur. Rhes. 816 (oath, Ζεὺς and πατήρ separated by the verb), AVŚ 6.120.s4 (dyaur + pitā, with bhūmir + mātā in the preceding verse), Cato Agr. 132.2 and 134.3 (vocative Iupiter in sacrificial prayer, alongside the vocative of Janus with pater). Exact cognates in all three branches: Ζεύς = dyáuḥ = Iu- (*dyḗws), πατήρ = pitā́ = -piter (*ph₂tḗr), in apposition naming the sky-god; Latin has univerbated the vocative into the theonym. Same referent, same title, same prayer/oath register; not generic (no generic reason for the sky to be the god systematically called 'father' in three branches) and not derivative (Cato's prayers are native Roman ritual). The Latin anchor carries the formula only in the fused name, which is itself the evidence of an old fixed phrase.

support: RV 7.81.3a, 7.81.5c, 8.47.14b, 10.70.6a (38 RV padas with div- + duhitár-)
cognate: Ved. diváḥ (gen. of dyú-/div-) = Gk Διός < *diwós; Ved. duhitár- = Gk θυγάτηρ < *dʰugh₂tḗr
drift_or_renewal: referent drift: in the RV the 'daughter of heaven' is Uṣas (Dawn); in Homer the same title goes to Aphrodite, Athena, Ate, Persephone, Artemis. Word order is free in both (diváḥ duhitā́ / duhitar divaḥ; Διὸς θυγάτηρ / θυγάτηρ Διός).
review: Passages: RV 1.92.5d (Dawn as diváḥ + duhitā́), Il. 4.515 (Athena) and Il. 3.374 (Aphrodite) with Διὸς + θυγάτηρ. Exact cognates: diváḥ = Διός (*diw-és/-ós), duhitár- = θυγάτηρ (*dʰugh₂tḗr), in the same relation (genitive of the sky-god + 'daughter') as a fixed honorific title of a goddess in verse, frequent on both sides (38 RV padas; many Homeric lines). The shift of referent (Dawn vs Aphrodite/Athena etc.) is a defensible drift of a title. Not generic (no language forms 'daughter of the sky' as a title by default) and not derivative.

cognate: *peḱu- 'livestock' (Lat. pecua, Ved. paśu-, Av. pasu-, Umbr. pequo) paired with *wiHro- 'man' (Ved. vīra-, Av. vīra-, Umbr. ueiro)
drift_or_renewal: Latin renews *wiHro- with pastores (Umbrian ueiro keeps it); in the slab's Vedic lines the pair is spread over livestock lists (go, aśva, aja, avi) + vīra/puruṣa, and AVŚ 11.2.18 counts puruṣa among the five paśavaḥ
phrase: *wiHrōs peḱu ... (salwom) servā- : 'keep men and cattle safe'
review: Anchors: Cato Agr. 141.3 (the full LASLA unit has pecua and salua with seruassis, beside pastores, in Mars' lustration prayer, before the address to Mars as pater); AVŚ 12.2.s29 (horses, men=vīreṣu, cows, goats, sheep), AVŚ 11.2.s45 (cows, men=puruṣeṣu), AVŚ 11.2.s18 (puruṣa among the five paśavaḥ). The anchors carry the merism only partly (Latin renews 'men' with pastores; the AV lines use vīra + go, or paśu + puruṣa). The exact pair is in support and checked: Umbrian Iguvine prayer (Buck 1904, ueiro + pequo with salua + seritu, which matches the Latin salua + seruassis), Avestan CAB YtFra2.10 (protection of pasuuā̊ + vīraiiā̊), YtZam8.3 (pasu + vīra 'undying'), AVP 19.56 (paśubhiś + vīraiḥ, refrain), AVŚ 11.1. Cognates exact: *peḱu- (pecu, paśu-, pasu-, pequo) and *wiHro- (vīra-, ueiro). Same speech act in three branches: a prayer that men and cattle be kept safe. A men-and-cattle merism is natural for herders, but the identical lexical pair in a fixed protective-prayer frame across Italic and Indo-Iranian goes beyond that. Accepted on the support; the anchors alone would be weak.

cognate: Gk ὠκύς = Ved. āśú- = Av. āsu- (*h₂ōḱú-); Gk ἵππος = Ved. áśva- = Av. aspa- (*h₁éḱwo-); Gk ζεύγνυμι, ζυγόν = Ved. yuj- (*yewg-)
drift_or_renewal: none for the core pair; Vedic often uses āśú- on its own for the yoked steeds (RV 1.118.4, 1.140.4); the chariot word differs (Gk ἅρμα vs Ved. rátha-)
review: Passages: Il. 23.294, 16.148, 24.14 (ὠκέας + ἵππους as object of yoking, ζυγόν/ζεύξειεν); RV 1.118.4b and 1.140.4d (the swift ones, āśávaḥ, yoked to the chariot), AVP 19.34.s24 (race charm, āśīyān + aśva). Support checked: RV 1.117.9b = 7.71.5b āśúm + áśvam; Avestan CAB has the compound āsu.aspa- 'having swift horses' (3 times). Exact cognates: ὠκύς = āśú- = āsu-, ἵππος = áśva- = aspa-, with *yewg- (ζεύγνυμι/ζυγόν = yuj-) in the yoking context on both sides. The adjective is one of several possible words for 'fast' in each language, and the noun-epithet pair is fixed (35 Homeric lines, several RV padas, a lexicalised Avestan compound). 'Swift horses' is semantically natural (medium generic risk), but the same epithet root in a fixed pairing and a compound in three branches is not chance.

cognate: Gk Ζεύς/Διί = Ved. dyáuḥ = Lat. Iu- (Iupiter) < *dyḗws; Gk πατήρ = Ved. pitā́ = Lat. -piter < *ph₂tḗr
drift_or_renewal: none (Latin has fused the vocative phrase *dyeu ph₂ter into the theonym Iupiter)
review: Passages: h.Ven. 29 (πατὴρ + Ζεύς), h.Ap. 307 (Διὶ + πατρί), AVŚ 6.120.s4 (dyaur + pitā), AVŚ 2.28.s7 and 9.10.s23 (dyauṣ/dyaur + pitā paired with pṛthivī + mātā), Cato Agr. 132.2 (vocative Iupiter in the daps prayer). Exact cognates in three branches (*dyḗws, *ph₂tḗr), same apposition naming the sky-god as father, Latin fused into the theonym; same religious register. Not generic, not derivative. Same evidence and grade as the other Father-Sky claim whose anchors carry the formula.

cognate: Ved. āmá- ~ Gk ὠμός 'raw' (*h₂eh₃mó-) qualifying Ved. kravís- ~ Gk κρέας 'raw flesh, meat' (*kréwh₂-s); verb of eating Ved. ad- ~ Gk ἔδω (*h₁ed-); and the compound 'raw-eater' Ved. āmā́d- ~ Gk ὠμηστής (*h₂eh₃mo- + *h₁ed-).
drift_or_renewal: Head noun partly renewed in AVŚ 8.6.48 (āmaṃ māṃsam, with kraviḥ in the parallel colon); RV 1.162.10 keeps the full pair āmásya kravíṣaḥ. Vedic kravís- narrowed to 'raw/bloody flesh, gore', Greek κρέας generalised to 'meat'. Verb of cooking renewed (Ved. pac-, Gk ἕψω/ὀπτάω).
review: Passages: AVŚ 8.6.s48 (demons who eat raw flesh: āmaṃ + māṃsam + adanti, with kraviḥ in the parallel colon); Hippocr. De prisca medicina 13 (sentence read: boiled instead of raw meat, ὠμῶν + κρεῶν, as the step from a crude diet). Support checked: RV 1.162.10b āmásya + kravíṣaḥ; Il. 22.347 (Achilles: raw meat, κρέα, to eat, ἔδμεναι); AVŚ 11.10.s18 (raw-eating vultures on a corpse). Exact cognates: āmá- = ὠμός, kravís- = κρέας, ad- = ἔδω; and the dedicated compound ὠμηστής = āmā́d- 'raw-eater' (Beekes s.v. ὠμός notes the Skt. match), used on both sides of beasts or demons feeding on the dead. The pairing with the same value (raw flesh as the food of the savage and demonic, set against cooked) recurs in both. 'Raw meat' alone would be generic, but the matching compound and context go beyond that.

cognate: agent noun *deh3-tor- (Ved. dātár-, Gk δώτωρ/δωτήρ, Av. dātar-) + gen. pl. of *h1wesu- 'good (things)' (Ved. vásūnām, Gk ἑάων, Av. vohunąm); god-word *deywós beside it in Vedic
drift_or_renewal: Greek ἐΰς survives only as adjective/gen. pl. ἑάων 'goods'; in the slab partners the Vedic side varies the verb (ā́ dade 'took to himself' in RV 7.6.7a; sāviṣad 'impel' with vasu-pati in AVP 19.1.5) while the exact agent-noun formula is RV 8.51.5 dātā́ vásūnām
phrase: *deh3tores h1wesuHom 'givers of goods' (Gk δωτῆρες ἑάων ~ Ved. dātā́ vásūnām ~ Av. dātārō vohunąm)
review: Anchors verified. Od. 8.335 has the exact agent noun + gen. pl. of *h1wesu- (also Od. 8.325, of the gods). RV 8.51.5a dātā́ + vásūnām and Av. Y16.1b, Y65.12b and Y65.13b dātar- + vohunąm match it exactly (both members cognate, same syntax, divine epithet in hymnic address). Greek ἐΰς is a living adjective in Homer, but its substantive 'goods' sense is confined to this genitive plural, a fossil that argues against independent creation. Caveats: the Vedic anchors RV 7.6.7a (ā́-dā- 'take') and AVP 19.1.5 (vasupati-) are only loosely related, and Av. dātar- could be 'creator' (*dʰeh1-).

cognate: *péḱu 'cattle' (Lat. pecua; Ved. paśú-, Av. pasu-, Umbr. pequo in support) in the merism *wiHro- peḱu 'men and cattle'
drift_or_renewal: renewal in both slab anchors: Latin pastores replaces *wiHro- (Umbrian keeps ueiro pequo, with saluo seritu = Cato salua seruassis); the AV verse renews both members (go- 'cows' for paśu-, puruṣa- for vīra-), keeping the frame 'welfare (svasti ~ salus) for family, cattle and men'. The cognate pair itself appears only in support (AVP paśubhiś ca vīraiḥ, Av. pasuuā̊ vīraiiā̊)
phrase: *wiHro- peḱu 'men and cattle' kept safe (Lat. salua seruare, Umbr. saluo seritu, Av. ϑrāϑrāi)
review: Anchors verified (Cato 141.3; AVS 1.31.7; AVP 1.22.7). The anchors are renewed (Latin pastores for *wiHro-; the AV verse has go- and puruṣa-), but the formula is solidly attested in the support, which I checked. Umbrian Iguvine Tables VIa 30-32 (Buck lines 14789-14820) have ueiro + pequo as beneficiaries with saluo + seritu, the same cognate verb and adjective as Cato's salua + seruassis. Av. YtFra2.10e and VrS18.3c have pasu- + vīra- for protection and peace. AVP 19.56 s26, s30 and s32 have paśu- + vīra- in a well-being prayer. Both members are cognate in coordination, in prayers for protection of a community, across Italic and Indo-Iranian. The Cato anchor keeps *peḱu and the protection frame. The merism is plausible among herders, but the agreement extends to the verb and adjective of keeping safe (in Italic).

words.etymon: unmapped (context-after line of the cited passage; = *h₂eh₃mó- 'raw' + *h₁ed- 'eat')

cognate: Gk ὠμός = Ved. āmá- (*h₂eh₃mó- 'raw'); Gk κρέας = Ved. kravís- (*kréwh₂s 'raw flesh'); Gk ἔδ-/ἐσθ- = Ved. ad- (*h₁ed- 'eat'); nominal compound Gk ὠμ-ηστής 'raw-eater' = Ved. āma-ád- 'raw-eater' (RV 10.87.7), with the parallel Ved. kravy-ád- 'flesh-eater' built on the cognate of κρέας.
drift_or_renewal: AVŚ 8.6.48 renews 'flesh' with māṃsa- (āmaṃ māṃsam adanti) beside kraviḥ in the same line; Greek κρέας has generalised to 'meat' and needs ὠμά to keep the 'raw' sense; Greek -ηστής is a new agent formation on *h₁ed- where Vedic keeps the root noun -ád-.
phrase: *h₂eh₃mo-h₁ed- 'raw-eater' / *h₂eh₃móm kréwh₂s h₁ed- 'eat raw flesh' (ὠμηστής ~ āmā́d-; ὠμὰ κρέα ἔδμεναι ~ āmaṃ ... kraviḥ adanti)
review: Anchors verified (Il. 22.66, with ὠμησταί in line 67; AVS 8.6.48; RV 1.162.10b; AVS 8.4.4). ὠμός = āmá- and the root *h1ed- are exact. The decisive match is the compound 'raw-eater' (Gk ὠμηστής, Ved. āmā́d-) with the same use: in RV 10.87.7d the raw-eating birds are to devour the sorcerer; in Il. 11.454 and 22.67 the raw-eating birds and dogs tear the enemy's corpse. Same scene and curse register, and both members cognate in the same order. Vedic kravyā́d- (flesh-eater; RV 7.104.2, 10.87.2/19) is the parallel compound on the cognate of κρέας. Caveat: the Greek agent formation in -ηστής differs from the Vedic root noun, and 'raw-eater' compounds are easy to coin, so the risk is medium.

cognate: *még̑h₂ ~ máhi ~ μέγα (here the superlative μέγιστον); *ḱléwos ~ śrávas ~ κλέος
drift_or_renewal: Pindar uses the superlative μέγιστον for the positive μέγα. The verb differs: Ved. ā́ dade 'took' (and elsewhere dhā-, rā-), Gk αὔξων 'increasing'. Ved. vardh- with śrávas (RV 8.15.8) is the semantic counterpart, not a cognate.
review: Anchors verified (RV 9.61.10c; Pindar I. 7.29). Neuter máhi = μέγα and śrávas- = κλέος are exact in form, and the attributive neuter noun phrase is formulaic on both sides: máh- + śrávas- in 16 RV pādas (1.8 expected; 11 with exactly the two words), μέγας + κλέος in 13 Homeric lines (1.7 expected; Il. 6.446, Od. 1.240). In both, fame is a prize won or increased. 'Great fame' is semantically natural, but the agreement in both the form and the noun phrase, with fame as a poetic value, makes this the clearest match in the batch.

support: RV 10.87.16 / AVŚ 8.3.29 (av:AVŚ, 8, 3.s29 in this slab, B-5f6e0)
cognate: Ved. āma- = Gk ὠμός (*h₂eh₃mó- 'raw'); Ved. kravís- = Gk κρέας (*kréwh₂s 'raw flesh'); Ved. ad- = Gk ἔδω (*h₁ed- 'eat'); agent compounds Ved. āmā́d- ~ Gk ὠμηστής (*h₂eh₃mo-h₁ed-) and kravyā́d-
drift_or_renewal: In the AV line āma- qualifies the inherited Indo-Iranian māṃsá- (*mḗms), and kravís- stands as a second object ('human kravis'); Greek has the adjective directly on κρέα. So the three roots form one clause in both, not one identical NP.
review: All three roots are exact cognates: āma = ὠμός (*h₂eh₃mó-), kravís = κρέας, ad = ἔδω. The anchors check: AVŚ 8.6.48 has demons who eat raw human flesh, and Il. 22.347 has Achilles wishing to eat Hector raw. Both are cannibal savagery. What lifts this above ordinary 'eat raw meat' is the agent compound and the curse context: Ved. āmā́d- (RV 10.87.7d, with adantu) ~ Gk ὠμηστής (< ὠμός + *h₁ed-), used of carrion birds and dogs that tear the enemy's body (Il. 11.454, 22.67). I also found AVŚ 11.10.18, where raw-eating vultures (āmādaḥ, gṛdhrāḥ) are to tear (radantām) the corpse; it closely matches Il. 11.454, where ὠμησταί tear (ἐρύουσι). In AV, āma qualifies māṃsa, not kravis, so the NPs are not identical. Ordinary dietetic use exists (Hippocrates), so medium risk.

words.etymon: mer- (slab mapping; the text has a-mṛtān = amṛtān, *n̥mr̥tós)

cognate: Ved. a-mṛ́ta- ~ Gk ἄμβροτος < *n̥-mr̥-tó- 'immortal' (of gods); Ved. mártya- ~ Gk βροτός < *mr̥-tó- / *mor-tyo- 'mortal' = 'man'
drift_or_renewal: Greek has renewed the word for god (θεός for *deywó-, Ved. devá-) and in the antithesis mostly the immortal pole (ἀθάνατος beside inherited ἄμβροτος); the Plato anchor (quoting Aeschylus) keeps only the mortal pole βροτοῖς opposite θεός. Vedic keeps both cognate poles
review: amṛ́ta- = ἄμβροτος (*n̥-mr̥-tó-) as an epithet of gods, against a *mer- word for men (mártya-, from *mórto-, vs βροτός *mr̥tó-; same root, different grade and suffix). The Vedic anchors carry both poles in one clause (AVP 1.78.1 devāṁ + amṛtān + martyaḥ; AVŚ 6.41.6 amartyā + martyāṁ; also RV 4.2.1, RV 10.91.11). The Greek anchor is weaker: Plato quotes Aeschylus, the god word θεός is not cognate, and only the mortal pole βροτοῖς appears. The Homeric support confirms the figure (Il. 24.460 θεὸς + ἄμβροτος; 24.464 ἀθάνατον + βροτούς; Od. 5.218). Calling men 'mortals' and gods 'immortals' with the *mer- root is a specific lexical choice, not a universal one. The god word is renewed in Greek.

support: Il. 15.46 (πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε); 41 Homeric lines with Ζεύς + πατήρ
cognate: *dyéw- + *ph₂tér-: Ved. dyaúṣ pitā́, Gk Ζεῦ πάτερ (cf. Lat. Iuppiter, from outside the slab)
drift_or_renewal: Vedic dyaúḥ is still the sky deified and is paired with Earth as mother (pr̥thivī́ mātā́); in Greek Ζεύς is a personal god and the pair is a fixed vocative of address
review: *dyéw- + *ph₂tér: Ved. dyaúḥ + pitā́ = Gk Ζεῦ + πάτερ = Lat. Iuppiter. An exact two-member cognate collocation in apposition, used of the sky god in prayer, and specific (the deified sky named as father). Exact vocative match in RV 6.51.5a (dyaùḥ + pítar). Note: neither anchor passage line contains the formula. It sits in the context lines (RV 1.191.6a, Il. 1.503), both checked.

cognate: Gk ὄνομα = Ved. nā́man- (*h₁nómn̥); Gk τίθημι = Ved. dhā- (*dʰeh₁- 'put'); Lat. nomen with in-dō (*en-dʰeh₁-). Recalled, not found in the lemmatized corpora (Hittite name-giving is mostly logographic there): Hitt. lāman dai- 'put a name' in narrative naming of a newborn (e.g. Song of Ullikummi). Incidentally the son word is cognate in the two anchors too: υἱεῖς ~ sūnúḥ (*suHnús).
drift_or_renewal: none in Greek/Vedic: both keep *h₁nómn̥ + *dʰeh₁-, and both in the middle voice (ἐθέμην, θέτο, τίθεσθ̓ ~ dadhé, dádhānaḥ). Latin keeps the verb only in the compound in-dere; the simplex 'nomen dare' (*deh₃- 'give') is a rival, renewed expression. In Vedic the collocation extends to a god's taking a name for fame (śrávase with nā́ma dadhé; śrávaḥ dadhiṣe nā́ma in RV 10.28.12).
review: ὄνομα = nā́man- (*h₁nómn̥) and τίθημι = √dhā (*dʰeh₁-), with the name as direct object, in the middle voice in both. Checked: Demosthenes Macart. 74 (ὀνόματα/ὄνομα + ἐθέμην, naming sons; everyday prose usage), RV 1.103.4d (nā́ma + dadhé), plus Od. 19.403/406 and 18.5 (naming a newborn), RV 10.115.2a, RV 5.3.10a, and Latin nomen + indo (PlCapt 69). Choosing 'put' over 'give/call' recurs in at least three branches. The Hittite lāman dai- is recalled and not verified. The Vedic anchor differs a little in sense (Indra takes a name for fame), but naming with dhā is also attested. *dʰeh₁- is a very general verb, so medium generic risk.

support: Il. 1.503, 12.164, 13.631 (41 lines with Ζεῦ πάτερ in Homer)
cognate: *dyew- 'Sky (god)' + *ph₂tér 'father': Ved. dyaúṣ pitā́ (voc. dyaùṣ pítar), Gk Ζεῦ πάτερ, Lat. Iū-piter
drift_or_renewal: Latin univerbates the vocative phrase into the name Iuppiter; Greek keeps it as a two-word invocation; Vedic keeps it as a two-word epithet, mostly paired with pṛthivī mātā
review: Same formula as B082 and B109: Ved. dyaúḥ + pitā́ (AVŚ 9.10.23, 6.120.4) = Gk Ζεῦ + πάτερ = Lat. Iuppiter (*dyew-ph₂ter, univerbated). Exact vocative in RV 6.51.5a. Anchor problems: in the Homeric anchors (Il. 15.371, 15.373) the formula is only in context line 15.372 (checked). AVŚ 6.120.3 has bhūmir + mātā, while dyaur + pitā is in s4. Catul 66.29 is irrelevant, and its context line 66.30 (Iupiter) is a translation of Callimachus, so it is derivative and adds nothing. Cato's Iane + pater and 'Iupiter' (CatAgr 134.2) are the real Latin witness. The claim is true despite these weak anchors.

words.etymon: dyew- (not listed by the slab mapping)
*dyew- + *ph₂tḗr (vocative compound; in the passage's context line, not word-listed)

cognate: Ved. dyauṣ (pitā) ~ Lat. Iou-/Iu-piter < *dyēws, *dyew-; Ved. pitā ~ Lat. -piter < *ph₂tḗr
drift_or_renewal: Latin has fused the vocative phrase *dyew ph₂ter into one theonym (Iūpiter), with oblique cases built on the bare stem (Iovi); Vedic keeps the two words free (dyauṣ ... pitā), separated by the clitic te/tvā
phrase: *dyēus ph₂tēr 'Sky Father' (Ved. dyauṣ pitā ~ Lat. Iupiter)
review: Ved. dyauṣ + pitā (AVP 1.12.5, AVŚ 2.28.7, long-life charms with pṛthivī + mātā) ~ Lat. Iupiter < *dyew + *ph₂ter, fused into a theonym with oblique Iou-. The Cato unit CatAgr 132.1 contains Ioui and the vocative Iupiter (dapalis) in a prescribed prayer at an offering. The Latin evidence is the fusion itself: an old apposition explains it, generic god + 'father' does not. Greek Ζεῦ + πάτερ (Il. 1.503) confirms. Context comparable (ritual address).

cognate: Ved. nā́man- = Gk ὄνομα (*h₁nómn̥); Ved. √dhā = Gk τίθημι (*dʰeh₁-); both verbs in the middle voice in the anchors (dádhānaḥ / τίθεσθε)
drift_or_renewal: none in the lexemes. The middle voice differs in use: Vedic dádhānaḥ nā́ma means 'taking a name for oneself' (Indra); Greek τίθεσθε ὄνομα means 'give your own child a name'. Active and passive Vedic uses (dadhāti, dhāyi) match the Greek 'give a name' exactly
review: Same collocation as B087: τίθημι + ὄνομα = √dhā + nā́man, both cognate and in the same relation (name as object of 'put'), both often middle. Checked: RV 6.44.8c (dádhānaḥ + nā́ma), Od. 19.406 (τίθεσθ' + ὄνομ'), Od. 19.403, Od. 18.5, RV 10.115.2a (nā́ma + dhāyi, the name given), RV 5.3.10a. The Vedic middle means 'assume a name' and the Greek 'give a name', but the passive and active Vedic uses match the Greek. The Hittite witness is fragmentary or recalled. The general sense of *dʰeh₁- makes some independent formation possible, so medium risk.

cognate: Ved. vácas- = Gk ἔπος = Av. vacah- (*wékʷos; slab maps vácāṃsi to the root wekʷ-); Ved. √takṣ = Av. taš- = Gk τέκτων, τεκταίνομαι (*tetḱ-; slab maps takṣam to tḗtḱti and τεχνῶν to tetḱsneh₂)
drift_or_renewal: Greek keeps the root only in derivatives (τέκτων 'craftsman', denominative τεκταίνομαι). Avestan has frozen the collocation as a compound, vacas-tašti- 'strophe' (literally 'word-fashioning')
review: The cognates are exact: vácas- = ἔπος = Av. vacah- (*wékʷos), and √takṣ = Av. taš- = τέκτων, τεκταίνομαι (*tetḱ-). The collocation 'fashion words (like a carpenter)' is checked in all three branches: RV 6.32.1d (vácāṃsi + takṣam), Od. 14.131 (ἔπος + παρατεκτήναιο), Pind. P. 3.113 (ἐπέων + τέκτονες), and the Avestan compound vacastašti- (N15.1a, VrS36.4l). It is a specific metaphor, not generic. Caveat: the Greek anchor (Philebus 55e) is a false match (τεχνῶν and the idiom with ἔπος + εἰπεῖν). The proof is in the support.

support: Il. 8.88; Il. 8.254 (35 Homeric lines with ὠκύς + ἵππος)
cognate: *HoHḱu- 'swift' + *h₁éḱwo- 'horse': Ved. āśú- áśva-, Gk ὠκέες ἵπποι, Av. āsu.aspa- (compound)
drift_or_renewal: In Vedic āśú- is often used alone as a noun meaning '(swift) horse' (RV 2.31.2c āśávaḥ; 2.34.3b āśúbhiḥ, with áśvān in the line before); Avestan has it only in the bahuvrīhi āsu.aspa-.
review: āśú- = ὠκύς = Av. āsu- (*h₁oHḱú-) and áśva- = ἵππος = aspa- (*h₁éḱwo-). Both members are cognate in an attributive collocation: RV 1.117.9b (āśúm + áśvam), Il. 10.474 (ὠκέες + ἵπποι, 35 Homeric lines), and the Avestan compound āsu.aspa-, plus āśú- used substantively as 'steed' (RV 2.31.2c, 2.34.3b, with áśvān in 3a). Anchor note: RV 2.31.2c has āśávaḥ without áśva. 'Swift horses' is semantically natural, but the three-branch fixity (formula, compound, substantivised epithet) argues for an inherited phrase.

cognate: *dyḗws + *ph2tḗr (Ved. dyaúṣ pitā́, Gk Ζεὺς πατήρ / Ζεῦ πάτερ, Lat. Iuppiter < *dyew-ph2ter)
drift_or_renewal: none in the epithet; Vedic keeps the sky-father paired with Earth-mother (pṛthivī mātā), Greek Zeus is no longer the sky itself, Latin univerbates it
review: Same Sky-Father formula (dyaur/dyauṣ + pitā ~ Ζεύς + πατήρ ~ Iuppiter). Exact cognates, specific. The Vedic anchors check (AVŚ 9.10.23, AVP 1.12.5, with pṛthivī + mātā). Greek: Διὶ + πατρί is in the context line (Od. 24.518, a prayer before a cast), not in the passage line 24.519, which I checked.

cognate: *deh₃- 'give' (agent noun *deh₃-tor-/-ter-, root noun -dā-) + *h₁wésu- 'good(s)': Gk δώτωρ/δωτήρ ἑάων ~ Ved. dātā́ vásūnām, vasu-dā́-, vásu-dāvan-
drift_or_renewal: the Greek agent noun is fully cognate (δώτωρ ~ dātár-); ἐύς survives in Greek almost only in this genitive-plural formula ('of goods'), so the phrase keeps an otherwise lost noun use. In the slab's Vedic anchors 'giver' is the root compound vasu-dā́ḥ (AVŚ 12.1.44) or is renewed as vasu-pati 'lord of goods' + vasūni sāviṣat (AVP 19.1.5); the agent-noun form dātā́ vásūnām is in RV 8.51.5
phrase: *deh₃tōr h₁wesuHoHom 'giver of goods' (δωτῆρες ἑάων ~ dātā́ vásūnām)
review: δώτωρ/δωτήρ = dātár- (*deh₃-tor-), with genitive plural ἑάων ~ vásūnām (*h₁wesu-), as a divine epithet 'giver of goods'. Checked: Od. 8.335 (δῶτορ + ἑάων, a vocative to Hermes), Od. 8.325 (θεοί + δωτῆρες + ἑάων), and RV 8.51.5a (dātā́ + vásūnām). Greek ἐύς is otherwise almost lost as a noun, which suggests a fossil. The AV anchors are weaker: AVŚ 12.1 has the compound vasu + dāḥ for Earth; AVP 19.1.5 has vasu + patiḥ, a renewal. The formula itself holds, with congruent context (gods as givers of wealth).

words.etymon: unmapped in slab (word absent from the slab's word list; context-before line CatAgr 132.2 w1/2); analysis *dyew- + *ph₂tḗr

cognate: Ved. dyaúṣ pitā́ (nom.; voc. dyaùṣ pítar) = Lat. Iū-piter / Diēs-piter = Gk Ζεῦ πάτερ, all *dyéw- + *ph₂tḗr 'Sky (god)' + 'father'; both members cognate in all three branches
drift_or_renewal: Latin univerbated the (vocative) phrase *dyeu ph₂ter into a proper name Iupiter/Diespiter, with 'father' no longer transparent; the oblique cases use the bare stem (Ioui). Vedic keeps a free two-word phrase (nominative in the AV anchors, vocative in RV 6.51.5), Greek keeps it as a vocative address (support only: no slab Greek passage has it)
review: Sky-Father formula with both members cognate in three branches: AVŚ 3.23.6 and 9.10.23 (dyauḥ/dyaur + pitā, with pṛthivī + mātā), CatAgr 132.2 (Iupiter + dapalis and Ioui in a prescribed offering prayer, the univerbated *dyew-ph₂ter), and Gk Ζεῦ + πάτερ (Il. 1.503 support). Also Diespiter (PlCapt 909, checked). Ritual context in both. Exact and specific.

cognate: *dyew- 'sky, Sky-god' + *ph₂tér 'father': Ved. dyaúṣ/dyaùḥ pitā́/pítar ~ Gk Ζεῦ/Ζεὺς πάτερ/πατήρ ~ Lat. Iuppiter, Diespiter
drift_or_renewal: none in the core pair; Latin has fused it into one compound name (Iuppiter, Diespiter)
phrase: *dyew- ph₂tér 'Father Sky' (Ved. dyauṣ pitā / dyauṣ pitar ~ Gk Ζεῦ πάτερ)
review: The best-anchored Sky-Father claim. Vedic dyauś/dyaur + pitā (AVP 5.21.1 with pṛthivī + mātā, against fever; AVŚ 9.10.23). The Greek passage lines carry Ζεῦ + πάτερ as prayer openings (Il. 19.121, 5.421, Od. 7.331, Pind. I. 6.42). The vocative matches exactly: RV 6.51.5a dyaùḥ + pítar, and AVŚ 6.4 dyauṣ + pitar (checked). Lat. Iuppiter/Diespiter fused. Exact cognates, congruent function (invocation), specific.

support: Tab. Iguv. VIa (repeated prayer: ... nerf arsmo ueiro pequo castruo fri salua seritu)
cognate: Ved. paśú- = Av. pasu- = Umbr. pequo = Lat. pecu < *péḱu 'livestock'; Ved. vīrá- = Av. vīra- = Umbr. ueiro (Lat. vir) < *wiHró- 'man'
drift_or_renewal: Latin (Cato's lustration prayer) renews *wiHro- with pastores while keeping pecua; word order varies: Indo-Iranian 'cattle + men', Italic 'men + cattle'
phrase: Av. pasu vīra / Ved. paśubhiś ca vīraiḥ / Umbr. ueiro pequo 'cattle and men' (Lat. pastores pecuaque)
review: Both members are cognate across Indo-Iranian and Italic: paśú- = pasu- = Umbr. pequo = Lat. pecu (*péḱu), and vīrá- = vīra- = Umbr. ueiro (*wiHró-). The formula appears as a fixed pair in welfare prayers. Checked: Y9.4e (pasu + vīra, in Yima's age none died), VS10.18c (pasu + vīra), Y45.9d (pasūš + vīrə̄ṇg), AVP 19.56.26/30/32 (paśubhiś + ca + vīraiḥ, an oblation refrain), Umbrian ueiro + pequo ... salua + seritu (Buck), and Cato 141.3 pastores + pecuaque + salua + seruassis (man-word renewed). Same function in all of them, not a casual co-occurrence. Low risk.

cognate: Ved. āśú- = Gk ὠκύς (*h₁ōḱú-, slab: HéHḱus); Ved. áśva- = Gk ἵππος (*h₁éḱwos), the noun appearing in Greek only in support passages
drift_or_renewal: none in the core formula. In the Greek slab anchor the epithet sits with another noun (βέλος ὠκύ 'swift missile'), and the horse formula ὠκέες ἵπποι is in support only. In RV 10.68.2d āśú- is used substantivally for racehorses ('like swift ones at the race').
review: āśú- = ὠκύς and áśva- = ἵππος are exact cognates. RV 10.107.10a really has áśvam, āśúm in agreement, of a racehorse groomed for the patron. Homer has ὠκύς, ἵππος in 35 lines (Il. 10.474, 10.527, 11.127 checked; the expected count by chance is about 2), and the RV has 9 stanzas with both against about 1.7 expected (RV 1.117.9, 7.71.5, 10.78.5 checked). Both use the adjective of chariot and race horses. Avestan names with āsu-, aspa- add a third branch. The Greek anchor Il. 14.407 is a misfit: ὠκύ goes with βέλος. RV 10.68.2d has āśū́n used as a noun with no horse word. So the case rests on the RV 10.107 anchor and the support. Swift horses is a natural phrase, but the frequency and fixed epithet status on both sides go well beyond chance.

cognate: Ved. dyaùḥ/dyaúḥ = Gk Ζεῦ(ς) < *dyēws; Ved. pítar/pitā́ = Gk πάτερ < *ph₂tér/*ph₂tḗr
drift_or_renewal: none in wording; in Vedic Dyaus is a receding figure paired with Earth-mother (merism dyaúḥ pitā́ pṛthivī́ mātā́), in Greek Zeus is the head of the pantheon. Latin fused the vocative into Iūpiter (recalled).
review: dyaùḥ = Ζεῦ (*dyēw-) and pítar = πάτερ (*ph₂ter) are exact. RV 6.51.5a is a true vocative pair with the second word unaccented, inside a prayer for mercy. Il. 19.121 is Hera's address to Zeus opening with Ζεῦ, πάτερ. Same speech act, same word order, same vocative syntax. Latin Iuppiter univerbates the same vocative. Not generic: a specific theonym, kin term, attested in three branches. RV 1.89.4b is the nominative variant inside the Sky-Earth merism. Homer has Ζεύς, πατήρ in 79 lines against about 10 expected.

cognate: Ved. vácas- = Gk ἔπος (*wékʷos, neuter s-stem, exact; slab maps vácas- only to the root *wekʷ-); ἄκουσας stands in the line after the slab passage; Ved. √śru- (śr̥ṇavat, śr̥ṇotu) = Gk κλύω (ἔκλυες, Il. 16.236/14.234) (*ḱlew-); 1sg possessor (Ved. gen. me / Gk ἐμόν, ἐμάν)
drift_or_renewal: In Pindar the verb is renewed as ἀκούω (ἀρὰν ἄκουσας) inside a line that keeps ἔπος and the address to the Father; Homer keeps the cognate verb (ἐμὸν ἔπος ἔκλυες). Possessor: Vedic enclitic genitive me vs Greek possessive adjective.
review: Ved. vácas- = Gk ἔπος is an exact neuter s-stem (*wékʷos). √śru- = κλύω (*ḱlew-). Both have a 1sg possessor. Homer has it exactly: Il. 16.236 has ἔπος as object of ἔκλυες, with the possessive ἐμόν, in Achilles' prayer to Zeus (verified), and Il. 14.234 has the same. The RV has the prayer formula of śr̥ṇavat with vácāṃsi and enclitic me in RV 10.66.11c, 1.145.3 and 10.65.13, all invoking gods to hear the poet. 8 RV stanzas have śru-, vácas- against about 3 expected. Same construction, same speech act, high-register 'word' on both sides. The Pindar anchor (I. 6.42) has ἔπος, ἐμάν next to Ζεῦ, πάτερ, but its verb is renewed (ἄκουσας) and it echoes Homer. RV 10.64.10b splits the verb (śr̥ṇotu) and the object vácaḥ across pādas. The Homeric support carries the claim.

support: Tabulae Iguvinae VIa 30-32 (Umbrian, in Buck 1904 text)
cognate: Lat. pecua = Umbr. pequo = Ved. paśú- = Av. pasu- < *péḱu 'livestock'; Lat. salua seruassis = Umbr. salua seritu (Italic, *solh2-wo- + *ser-w-); the human member *wiHro- survives in Umbr. ueiro, Av. vīra-, Ved. vīrá- (RV 10.85.44 vīrasū́ḥ in the same śám-formula stanza).
drift_or_renewal: Latin renews *wiHro- 'men (of the household)' with pastores (herdsmen) while keeping pecua; Vedic recasts the merism descriptively as dvipád- / cátuṣpad- 'two-footed / four-footed' (RV 1.121.3d adds náryāya 'manly' to the two-footed member), with paśú- surfacing beside it in RV 3.62.14.
phrase: *wiHro- *peḱu- (men and livestock) in a prayer for safety/health
review: The Latin anchor CatAgr 141.3 checks out: pastores and pecua kept salua by seruassis in Cato's lustration prayer to Mars. The Iguvine prayer in Buck's text has ueiro, pequo ... salua, seritu (the VIa 30-32 type, repeated several times). So Lat. pecu = Umbr. pequo and saluus, seruare = salua, seritu are exact cognate pairs in identical prayer contexts. Latin renews *wiHro- as pastores. The 'men, livestock' merism links outward through Av. pasu, vīra (Y 9.4e, VS 10.18c, YtMihr 29.2h; 12 CAB units). This is a sound inherited formula. Caveat: the Vedic anchor RV 1.121.4a is irrelevant (the merism is in 3d, with dvipád/cátuṣpad, different words and not a petition). RV 1.114.1c is the real Vedic analogue but is a lexical renewal. The core Latin-Umbrian agreement is Italic-internal.

words.etymon: unmapped in slab (proper noun not in word list); = univerbated *dyew- (voc. *dyéw) + *ph₂tḗr

cognate: Gk Ζεύς / Ved. dyáuḥ / Lat. Iou- (Iu-piter) < *dyḗws; Gk πατήρ / Ved. pitā́ / Lat. -piter (pater) < *ph₂tḗr. Every member of the pair is cognate in all three branches; Latin has univerbated the vocative phrase *dyéw ph₂ter into the theonym Iuppiter (Diespiter).
drift_or_renewal: none in Greek and Vedic; in Latin the phrase has been fused into a single name (univerbation), with pater still separately usable in prayer (Iane pater, CatAgr 134.3)
review: Same inherited formula as B113. AVŚ 3.23.14 and 9.10.23 have dyauḥ, pitā beside pṛthivī, mātā (9.10.23 = RV 1.164.33), and Cato Agr. 132.2 has the univerbated vocative Iupiter in a sacrificial address. Fully regular cognates in three branches, and the RV vocative (RV 6.51.5a) matches Ζεῦ, πάτερ. Caveats: the Aristotle anchor (Pol. 1259b) only quotes Homer's 'father of men and gods' for Zeus. It is derivative and not the appositional formula itself. In Latin, Iuppiter is a fused name, not a free phrase. The grade rests on the Vedic and Homeric material.

cognate: Gk ὄφις = Ved. áhi- = Av. aži- < *h₁ógʷʰis (object noun); Ved. han- / Av. jan- < *gʷʰen- (verb)
drift_or_renewal: renewal: Greek replaces *gʷʰen- (θείνω, πέφνον, φόνος) by κτείνω in the dragon-killing sentence; the object noun stays cognate
phrase: *gʷʰent h₁ógʷʰim 'slew the serpent' (Gk with renewed verb)
review: Ved. ahann, ahim (AVŚ 2.5.11 = RV 1.32.2) and Av. janat̰, ažīm (Y 9.8a, 9.11a, checked) are exact cognates on both elements (*gʷʰen-, *h₁ógʷʰi-), in the same mythic act: a hero slays the serpent. Pindar P. 4.249 has κτεῖνε ... ὄφιν (Jason slays the guardian serpent). ὄφις is the exact cognate of the object, and the verb is renewed with κτείνω, a renewal of a well-known kind. The RV pair is formulaic (30 stanzas with áhi-, han- against about 2.7 expected). This meets the threshold: an exact Indo-Iranian pair plus the Greek object cognate in the same clause shape and context.

cognate: Gk ὄνομα = Ved. nā́man- = Av. nąman- = Lat. nōmen < *h₁nómn̥; Gk τίθημι (mid. τίθεμαι) = Ved. dhā- (mid. dadhe) = Av. (fra-)dā- = Lat. -dere in in-dere < *dʰeh₁- 'put, set'
drift_or_renewal: none in Greek/Indo-Iranian; Latin keeps the root only in the compound in-dere (nōmen indere), the simplex having merged into dare/-dere
review: ὄνομα = nā́man- = nąman- = nōmen and τίθημι = dhā- = Av. dā- = Lat. -dere (in-dere) are exact. Every anchor has the collocation with 'name' as direct object of *dʰeh₁-, mostly middle. Plato Theages 122d: ὄνομα, ἔθου, the father naming his son. RV 1.103.4d: nā́ma, dadhé, the son taking a name. AVŚ 5.1.6: dadhete, nāma. Also Sophist 225a and Phaedrus 267d. Supported by Od. 19.403-6, Vd 18.52 and Plautus nomen with indere. The choice of 'put' for naming, rather than 'call', recurs in at least four branches, with matching middle voice. Same verdict as B148.

cognate: Ved. āmá- 'raw' = Gk ὠμός (*h₂oh₃mó-); Ved. kravís- 'raw flesh' = Gk κρέας (*krewh₂-s); Ved. ad- = Gk ἔδ- (ἔδμεναι, -ηστής, ἐδεστής) (*h₁ed- 'eat')
drift_or_renewal: Vedic keeps kravís- as a marked word for raw/gory flesh and builds the verb phrase into agent compounds (āmā́d-, kravyā́d-); Greek uses the ordinary κρέας 'meat' and builds parallel agent formations ὠμηστής, κρεῶν ἐδεστής (parallel compounding, not an exact equation: suffixes differ). AVŚ 8.6.48 renews the noun once with māṃsa- (āmaṃ māṃsam) beside kraviḥ.
phrase: *h₂oh₃mó- *krewh₂- *h₁ed- 'eat raw flesh' — Ved. āmaṃ ... adanti ... kraviḥ ~ Gk ὠμῶν κρεῶν; ὤμ̓ ... κρέα ἔδμεναι
review: āmá- = ὠμός, kravís- = κρέας and ad- = ἔδω are all exact cognates. AVŚ 8.6.48 really has āmaṃ, adanti and kraviḥ in one clause, of demons eating raw (human) flesh, and RV 1.162.10b has āmásya, kravíṣaḥ. Il. 22.347 has all three Greek reflexes in one line (ὤμ', κρέα, ἔδμεναι): Achilles' wish to devour Hector raw. Herodotus 3.99 (ἐδεσταί of raw κρεῶν, cannibals) also checks. The contexts agree: savage or demonic eating of human flesh. Vedic keeps the inherited *krewh₂- in this marked 'raw flesh' sense beside ordinary māṃsa-, and both sides build raw-eater agent nouns. The Hippocratic anchor is a mere dietary use, but the three-term match in congruent contexts is beyond chance (Homer has 1 line with ὠμός, κρέας).

words.etymon: déh₃- (or dʰeh₁-; Avestan dā- merges both)

cognate: Gk δίδωμι, δωτήρ, δώτωρ = Av. dā-, dātar- = Ved. dā-, dātár- (*deh₃-); Gk ἐΰς gen.pl. ἑάων = Av. vohu- = Ved. vásu- (*h₁wésu- 'good, goods')
drift_or_renewal: none in the lexemes. The slab anchors show the finite-verb form (δίδωσι ... ἑάων; dā̊s ... yā vohū); the agent-noun formula proper (*doh₃tōr h₁wesuom) is in the support loci.
review: *deh₃- 'give' and *h₁wésu- 'goods' are cognate: δίδωμι/δωτήρ = dā-/dātár- = Av. dā-/dātar-, and ἐύς (gen. pl. ἑάων) = vásu- = vohu-. The formula is solid in support: Od. 8.325 (gods as δωτῆρες, ἑάων) and 8.335 (δῶτορ, ἑάων) check; RV 8.51.5a (dātā́, vásūnām) checks; Y 65.12b (vohunąm, dātārō, of the Aməṣ̌a Spəṇtas) and Y 16.1b (dātārəm, vohunąm) check. The archaic ἑάων is confined to this formula. The anchors are partial. Il. 24.528 has δίδωσι with ἑάων (Zeus's jars), which is congruent. Y 39.4 dā̊s may be *dʰeh₁- rather than *deh₃- (Avestan merges them), and AVŚ 7.97.8 gives only vasūni. Accepted on the agent-noun formula, which is triple and exact.

support: Hittite lāman dai- 'give a name' (recalled, not searched)
cognate: *h₁nómn̥ (ὄνομα ~ nā́man-) as object of *dʰeh₁- 'put' (τίθημι ~ √dhā-); Latin nomen indere (in-dō < *en + dʰeh₁-) as a third branch
drift_or_renewal: none in the core; voice differs: RV 1.103.4 is reflexive middle (the son 'took a name' for fame), the Greek is indirect middle (the father 'set a name' for the child); RV 10.71.1 nāmadhéyaṃ dádhānāḥ ('giving names', the primal naming) and RV 5.3.10 active dadhāti close the gap
review: Same inherited collocation as B133, graded identically: *h₁nómn̥ as object of middle *dʰeh₁-. Isaeus 3.30 (ὄνομα, θέσθαι, the father naming the child at the tenth-day feast) and Dem. 43.74 (ὀνόματα, ἐθέμην for his sons) check, both naming a child, as does RV 1.103.4d (nā́ma, dadhé). The voice differs slightly (reflexive vs indirect middle), but the choice of 'put' for naming recurs across Greek, Indo-Iranian and Latin (nomen with indere). The prose anchors are late but represent ordinary Greek usage continuous with Od. 19.406.
